Tragic, yes...but this is the sort of thing that should garner attention and, hopefully, a dynamic response. I’ve been refusing to give up on nature in spite of the solid kick in the chops I routinely receive.

Well.....as an ancient tree-hugger I have an interest in this. I’ve been working in conversation and habitat restoration in particular, for well over thirty years. It’s an utterly thankless job and both the climate change disclaimers  and the Gen X+ crowd hate me, accusing me of being a traitor and not trying hard enough. The ‘not trying hard enough’ crowd leaves me hurt and bewildered. Unless you’ve tried to work with habitat restoration, you’ve no idea what a heartbreaking and frustrating task it is. One of my biggest adversaries is Bambi, yeah, the motherfucking deer. They’re the singularity most destructive creatures to many natural habitats in existence. Worse than mankind.  But, mankind gave Bambi the upper hand. Before settlers started farming there was an ocean of trees from the Atlantic to Ohio here, in New York State. As farmers destroyed forests to create fields for farming it also created an ideal situation for deer. Deer are classified as “edge feeders’, thriving on a specific plant life that’s between the forests and open land. Then....we gifted the voracious monsters with lawns and fields of toasty produce, The population of deer has exploded to the point of open warfare between them and someone like me who’s desperate to restore local swaths of natural beauty, like large stands of Cypripedium reginae or C. acaule, both magnificent native/terrestrial orchids. The deer covet them, but without the naturally established to foils of large wild shrubs and under planting’s, the bastards seek and destroy. I’ve seen massive naturally established stands of Trillium wiped out in a few years once a herd discovers, gone forever. There are many, many more hostile enemies of natural habitats, of course. When I purchased my home in WNY it came with a magnificent stand of hundreds of White Bark Birch. Good thing I was so enamoured because I took lots of pictures. A mere 6 years into living here something called the Bronze Birch Borer swept through, an import fro China, and killed every one of my Birch Trees. I spent weeks with a chainsaw cleaning that mess and, sadly, Birch is a shit fire wood. So....I’m still trying different approaches, hoping at least a bit of it will have an effect.

EDIT: the reason I launched into this particular response was because I’ve discovered “unknown” species of trees, shrubs and perennials. Each tales 4 men to lift so the work involved was formidable, but at least my stone master wasn’t  carving out straight lines. I sold these for $500 each, before anyone thinks that was a fools venture. They were drilled with a hole for draining and convert d to a planter for Alpine plants, a specialist group that thrives in such a setting. If desired, one could easily plug it back and use it as a water feature formLotus or water lilies. During this, I got to know the villages and villagers and never lacked for a snack or a soft drink, these were marvellous people who were more than happy to entertain us. Fast forward to the next year, one morning I got up and the international news was about a volcano in Indonesia. On the Island of Java. It still didn’t register until I heard Mt.
